set.approach: From the climbers' parking area beside the Icefields Discovery Centre, follow the service road used by the glacier tour vehicles, then leave it and climb the lateral moraine. The moraine path is loose and faint, shifts from year to year, and is marked in places by small cairns; it ends at a rock headwall with a few scrambling moves on loose rock. Above the headwall, put on crampons and rope up at the edge of the glacier. Serac fall and crevasses are the main concerns on the ice, so start early and check the forecast and current glacier reports before going.
set.descent_text: Two ways down are in use. One is the North Glacier route, which passes beneath the serac band above the glacier and so carries serac-fall exposure. The other goes back down the steep couloir below the Silverhorn, facing the slope and stepping carefully, and is generally considered the safer choice though longer and slower. Either way you finish with a long walk down the moraine and service road to the parking area. Both lines cross glacier terrain, so keep the rope on and watch for crevasses and avalanche on the couloir.

review.notes: Approach and moraine/headwall/glacier from both trip reports; descent options (North Glacier past the serac, or the couloir facing out) from the two reports. Neither gives a count so none stated.

review.notes: Shared approach only; the route's own top-out and descent not clearly stated, so no descent written.

set.approach: Park at the pullout on the Icefields Parkway beside Hector Creek; the glacier cannot be seen from the road. Follow the south side of the creek through a short band of forest, then climb the narrow gully into the large bowl below the glacier. This gully and bowl are avalanche terrain, so choose the day and the hour with care and cross it early. Above it the valley opens; angle toward the toe of the glacier and rope up there. Glacier travel precautions apply all the way, as the ice is crevassed.
set.descent_text: From the summit, scramble back down the third-class rock to the col, then go down the glacier the way you came, roped, keeping clear of crevasses and snow bridges. Stay well back from the edges of the ridge in early season because of cornices. The glacier ends at the avalanche-prone bowl and gully; descend that with the same care as on the way up and follow Hector Creek through the forest to the road. Skiers often take their skins off and ski the glacier and creek.

review.notes: Trailhead, creek, bowl and glacier from the route page and two trip reports; third-class scramble from route page; descent is the ascent reversed per the trip reports.

set.approach: Start at the gate on the Moraine Lake access road, which is closed to vehicles in winter and spring, and travel the road to the junction with the Paradise Valley trail. Continue toward Annette Lake, then bear left up the open bowl beneath the north face of Mount Temple. Travel to the col at the foot of Little Temple; the couloir rises directly above it. The couloir steepens and narrows as you climb and a cornice often sits at the top. The approach crosses avalanche terrain and passes under glacier and serac hazard from the north face, so check the avalanche forecast, and ask Parks Canada about any current trail restrictions.

review.notes: Single route page for the approach; second page confirms Moraine Lake road and Paradise Valley turn-off. Descent only described as a ski run, so none written.

set.approach: Take Highway 99 from Squamish to the Cheekye forest road and follow it and its Brohm Ridge branch as far as snow or the road end allows; conditions on these forest roads vary, so check ahead. From the end, climb to the crest of Brohm Ridge, which is well defined, and follow it east, staying low to avoid steep side slopes below rock towers. Drop onto the Warren Glacier and cross it, roped, then continue over the North Pitt Glacier to the flat bench at the foot of the northeast face. Crevasses and seracs are present and snowmobile traffic is common on the lower road.
set.descent_text: Go back down the northeast face by the way you came up, watching for the bergschrund and for cornices along the upper edges. Rope up again where the glaciers are crevassed, then retrace the route across the glaciers and west along Brohm Ridge. Late in the day the snow on the ridge can be sticky and the many small ups and downs slow progress. From the road end, follow the forest road out to the highway.

review.notes: Road, ridge and glacier route in all three; descent is the ascent reversed in the two trip reports.

set.approach: Take the Neffs Canyon trail until it levels and turns from road to trail. Cross the creek at the fork and follow the old pipeline road along the west fork. The trail leaves the creek and winds through trees; stay in the basin the creek has cut and you reach a waterfall, which you bypass on the east side (climber's left) to enter the couloir. Rattlesnakes and loose rock make the drainage unpleasant in summer, and access to the north side crosses private property in places, so check the current situation before you go. Carry an ice axe and possibly crampons.
set.descent_text: Reverse the couloir from the notch. Bum-sliding is popular in good snow, but the couloir has a secondary fall line that pulls you toward the west wall, where sun can open a moat that has caught experienced climbers. In good conditions you can slide from the notch to the waterfall, bypass it on the east side and walk out to Neffs Canyon. Rocks poke through the snow in places, so keep your axe in hand.

review.notes: Blades page for approach and descent; Reese page confirms the Blades descent hazards and Neffs Canyon walk out.

set.approach: Park at the end of Gilead Way. The old trail by the water tower is hard to reach without crossing private property, so the approach is a bushwhack to a creek crossing, then a game trail with a steep, often wet step and an easily missed fork to the right. The fork leads up a steep, muddy slope and through scrub oak to a small rock outcrop, where you drop west into the couloir. The drainage has loose rock and rattlesnakes in summer. The couloir is the prominent snow line in the middle of the north face. Take an ice axe, and crampons if you want them.
set.descent_text: Retrace the couloir from the summit ridge, or drop down Blades Couloir instead; rocks stick up through its snow. Bum-sliding is popular on Blades in good snow, and in good conditions you can slide from the notch to the waterfall, bypass it on the east side and walk out to Neffs Canyon. Keep away from the west side where sun forms a moat that can be dangerous.

review.notes: Reese page for approach and the two descents; Blades page confirms the Blades descent and moat hazard.

set.approach: Drive up Little Cottonwood Canyon a short way past the Lisa Falls trailhead to the Tanner's Gulch sign. Go past the sign and around a bend to a gravel pullout on the right when heading uphill. Cross the road, find the faint climbers' trail in the brush, and follow it to the gulch. Early in the season the gulch is filled with snow from low down; the lower part has easy mixed steps. Carry an ice axe and crampons, and check the avalanche forecast first, since the gulch is a funnel.
set.descent_text: The route ends at the saddle between Dromedary and Sunrise peaks. The last stretch below it may be snow, ice or a heavy cornice. Go back down the gulch the way you came, which is the usual choice on skis, or continue over the saddle and descend into Broads Fork to exit that way. Loose terrain makes the gulch unpleasant on foot when the snow is thin, and avalanche conditions matter either way.

set.approach: Drive up Pole Canyon Road out of Mona as far as your vehicle can go, or walk the rest of the road. Bushwhack generally southeast until you meet a drainage that is easy to follow up to Pole Canyon Basin; its avalanche path leads you into the basin, which has many chutes and a view of Nebo. Champagne Chute is the leftmost line as you look up at the peak and is much narrower than the northwest couloir. Take an ice axe, crampons, a helmet and avalanche gear.

review.notes: Single route page; no descent described.

set.approach: The couloir cuts the north side of the Twins above Gad Valley at Snowbird. Climb into the lower bowl below the face and up to the mouth of the diagonal couloir, which steepens as it goes. The face lies within the ski area's terrain, so ask about access and closures before going and check the avalanche forecast. Pickets can be useful later in the season when the snow firms up.

review.notes: Route page and area page; no descent described.

set.approach: Start at the Cog Railway lot, take the Ammonoosuc Link to the Ammonoosuc Ravine Trail, and follow the river on the flat, narrow trail until a small tributary crosses it. The stream is hard to spot unless there are tracks. Leave the trail there on your right, climb through open conifer glades to the foot of the slide, then follow the easy snow gully uphill. Snow here is often scoured by wind, so crampons are useful.
set.descent_text: The gully ends below the boulder-covered cone of Mount Monroe, so bear left toward the saddle between Washington and Monroe, where you can continue to either summit. Descend by way of the Ammonoosuc Ravine Trail, which also makes a good ski. Weather on the Presidentials changes fast, so check the forecast and avalanche advisory.

review.notes: Single route page plus area page for the trail context.

set.approach: The trail starts at the far end of the large gravel lot at the Arizona Snowbowl, off the Snowbowl Road, and passes beneath a chairlift before crossing a meadow. In the aspen and pine forest, keep left at the trail register; the right-hand fork heads for the ski lodge. A long series of switchbacks climbs through forest, with bristlecone pines appearing higher up, and then the trail leaves the trees at treeline. Stay on the path above treeline to protect the alpine plants, and the saddle between Humphreys and Agassiz lies near 11,800 feet. From the saddle the trail turns north to the summit, about a mile away.
set.descent_text: Go back down the way you came, the Humphreys Trail to the saddle and then the switchbacks to the Snowbowl lot. The upper trail is rocky and the loose stones are slippery underfoot, so take care on the way down. Lightning is a concern on the exposed ridge above treeline, so plan to be off it early in the day. Where snow lies on the upper mountain, an ice axe and traction are useful.

review.notes: Both pages: Snowbowl lot, meadow under lifts, switchbacks, treeline, saddle ~11,800 ft, summit about a mile north; return by the same trail. The lightning and snow-gear lines are general advice.

set.descent_text: Go back down the boulder ridge from the summit to Anderson Pass, which is class 2 with cliffs on the left to avoid. From the pass, return along the Henrys Fork trail the way you came, either over Gunsight Pass by the steep shortcut or by the longer, gentler line through Painter Basin. The trip is long, so plan the descent into the afternoon when thunderstorms are common above treeline, and start the summit push early.

review.notes: Both pages: out-and-back by the same trail; Gunsight shortcut and Painter Basin options; thunderstorm note from the second.

set.approach: Take the Profanity trail to roughly the 4,100-foot level, then traverse right (north) beneath the east face of the Chin, following the base of the rock face to the fan of snow at the bottom of the chute. The line drops directly from the summit; a steep snow slope funnels into a narrow couloir before opening onto a moderate slope. It needs good snow cover to fill in, and is best after a hard freeze at dawn. Carry an ice axe and avoid it on powder days because of avalanche risk. Check for seasonal raptor closures before going.

review.notes: Single route page; no descent described.
